resources.string: How long the same key keeps cycling before another tap starts a new letter. Nobody has to wait it out — ▶ ends a letter immediately — so a longer window costs nothing.

Remotes disagree about which buttons exist and about what they report. Press the button you want and it gets recorded. Only the first is worth assigning on most remotes: deleting is BACK while a letter is in progress, and every digit is also the last stop on its own key. Number keys cannot be assigned — they are the keyboard.
In use. Focus a text field and it comes up.
Enabled, but another keyboard is in use. Switch to this one below.
Not enabled yet. Android needs every keyboard turned on by hand — do that below, then switch to it.
Leaves this app. Enable or switch the active keyboard there.
The only thing here that uses the network. It runs in a separate process, only when you press it, and sends nothing. This keyboard stores nothing you type in the first place.

Number keys carry the letters. Tap 2 once for a, twice for b, three times for c — then ą, then ć, then the digit 2 itself. Every Polish letter is on the key its base letter is on, at the end of the run: ż is 9 tapped six times.

▶ ends the letter, so a doubled one needs no pause in the middle of a word. ◀ steps back if you tapped past the letter you wanted. OK finishes and searches, 0 adds a space, 1 cycles the punctuation a search box needs. BACK drops the letter in progress, then closes the keyboard.

Nothing here is predicted, so nothing here can be wrong. The presses for a word are the same today as they will be in a year, and you never have to read the screen to find out what the keyboard did with the last one.
Focus this field to bring the keyboard up. Nothing here is saved.
Press the key that should open the keyboard when it is hidden.
Without this the keyboard only appears when an app asks for it, which Netflix and YouTube do not always do.
Press the key that should delete.
Up already deletes, and always does. Assign a key only if you would rather not reach for the d-pad.
Press the key that should switch between letters and digits.
A field that wants a number switches on its own, and a digit is always the last stop on its own key. This only makes it one press instead of six.
The keyboard needs this button for typing, so it cannot be assigned. Choose again and press a different one.
The next button you press is the one taken. BACK cancels.
Nothing here takes text. Open a search box first.
The number keys, the letters on each, and where the taps have got to. The remote has nothing printed on it, so leave this on until you know the layout.
Just the run of letters for the key you are tapping. Assumes you know which key carries what.
The smallest strip there is. You lose nothing but the tap count — the letter in progress is in the field either way.
Multitap is open source and MIT licensed. It is free, it stays free, and nothing in it is locked away for people who do not pay.
If it has saved you a few thousand trips around an on-screen grid, you can buy me a coffee.
Multitap installs from its GitHub releases.
This repository has no releases yet.
Handing the file to the system installer.
Android stops an app when it replaces it, so this screen will close. The keyboard itself keeps working — reopen the app only to change settings.
The system asked for confirmation but did not say what to show.
Android needs your permission for this app to install packages.
Checked only when you press it. One request for the version, one for the file, nothing sent. What you type never leaves the device, and is never stored on it either.
